title: England Bans Deep-Fried Food from School Lunches
paragraphs: Schools in England will no longer serve deep-fried food to pupils at lunchtime, under new national standards for school meals designed to improve children's health.

The government first proposed the changes in April 2026 and asked the public for their views until June. The final standards were confirmed in September 2026. They will apply to state schools, including academies and free schools, from September 2027, while some requirements for secondary schools will be introduced from September 2028.

The most notable change is the ban on deep-fried food. Under the previous rules, schools were allowed to serve deep-fried food twice a week. In addition, the new standards restrict foods that are high in sugar, such as ice cream, waffles and sugary drinks. Fruit juice will be removed from primary schools, and desserts will be cut back. Other popular items, such as cake, chips, pizza and sausage rolls, will be available less often.

At the same time, the new standards place more emphasis on fruit, vegetables, pulses and whole grains. Main meals will need to include vegetables or salad, and every main dish must contain a source of protein. Bread will need to contain more fiber, and at least half of the pasta served will have to be wholewheat. For the first time, breakfast clubs will also have their own nutritional standards.

The government says the changes are needed because of concerns about children's health. Around one in three children in England leaves primary school overweight or obese. Furthermore, tooth decay linked to diets high in sugar is the leading cause of hospital admissions for children aged five to nine.
Nutritionist Rhiannon Lambert described the changes as a really positive and long-overdue step forward for children's nutrition in the UK.

However, some people have raised concerns. In one pilot project in Brighton, the number of pupils eating school meals fell by 15% after healthier food was introduced, and some pupils brought less healthy packed lunches instead. Others have questioned how schools will pay for the changes.
